Let $s\in(0,1)$, $N\geqslant 1$ and $A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ be a constant and symmetric matrix\footnote{
Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ be a constant matrix, and denote by
\[
A_{sym}:=\frac{A+A^T}{2},\quad A_{asym}:=\frac{A-A^T}{2}
\]
its symmetric and antisymmetric parts, respectively.

We notice that the bilinear form associated with~$A$ depends only on $A_{sym}$. Indeed, using the Fourier representation of the fractional gradient, we obtain that
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}A_{asym}D^su(x)\cdot D^sv(x)\,dx = C_{N,s} \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\xi|^{2s-2}\left(A_{asym}\xi\cdot\xi\right)
\widehat u(\xi)\widehat v(-\xi)\,d\xi.
\]
Since $A_{asym}^T=-A_{asym}$, we have that $A_{asym}\xi\cdot\xi=0$ for every~$\xi\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Therefore,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} A D^su(x)\cdot D^sv(x)\,dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}A_{sym}D^su(x)\cdot D^sv(x)\,dx.
\]
Hence, in the case of constant coefficient, we may assume without loss of generality that~$A$ is symmetric.

In addition, we have that $z\cdot Az=z\cdot A_{sym}z$ and~$\operatorname{tr}(A)=\operatorname{tr}(A_{sym})$,  so that the explicit representing kernel associated with~$A$ is the
same as that associated with $A_{sym}$.}. Let $k_A\in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta)$ and assume that~\eqref{lòkgyftdresdetfyguhijok} holds.

Then, 
the following statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] 
For every~$u,v\in\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^N)$,
\begin{equation*}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}A D^su(x)\cdot D^sv(x)\,dx = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}} (u(x)-u(y))(v(x)-v(y)) k_A(x, y)\,dx\,dy.
\end{equation*}

\item[(ii)]
For almost every~$x\ne y$,
\[
k_A(x,y) = \frac{c_{N,s}}{4s|x-y|^{N+2s}}\left((N+2s)\frac{(x-y)\cdot A(x-y)}{|x-y|^2}-\operatorname{tr}(A)\right).
\]
\end{enumerate}

Also, if either~$(i)$ or~$(ii)$ holds true, then
\begin{itemize}
\item \eqref{srdtfyguioplèòlkoijhugyftr2} is satisfied for all~$\eta\in(0,2s]$ and a suitable constant $M>0$,
 \item \eqref{srdtfyguioplèòlkoijhugyftr1} holds for some $\alpha\in(0,2)$ and~$0<\lambda\leqslant\Lambda<\infty$,  if and only if \eqref{tracecondition} holds, and in this case necessarily~$\alpha=2s$.

title: Proof
body_md:
By using~\eqref{defnfrgradient}
in combination with Plancherel's identity, and recalling that $D^s_j\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)$ for any $j\in\{1,\dots, N\}$, we infer that
\[
\begin{split}
&\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}D_k^s u(x) D_j^s v(x) dx =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}D_k^s u(x) \overline{D_j^s v(x)} dx =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \widehat{D_k^s u}(\xi)\overline{\widehat{D_j^s v}(\xi)}d\xi\\
&\qquad=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\bigl(i\xi_k|\xi|^{s-1}\widehat{u}(\xi)\bigr)\overline{\bigl(i\xi_j|\xi|^{s-1}\widehat{v}(\xi)\bigr)}\,d\xi=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\xi_k\xi_j|\xi|^{2s-2}\widehat{u}(\xi)\overline{\widehat{v}(\xi)}\,d\xi.
\end{split}
\]
Accordingly, by recalling~\eqref{BAdef1}, we get
\[
\mathcal{B}_A(u,v) =\sum_{j,k=1}^N A_{jk} \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}D_k^su(x) D_j^sv(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\xi|^{2s-2} \left(\sum_{j,k=1}^N A_{jk}\xi_j\xi_k\right)\widehat{u}(\xi)\overline{\widehat{v}(\xi)}\,d\xi,
\]
which is the desired result.

label: lemmauniq
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemmauniq}
Let $k_1,k_2\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta)$ satisfy~\eqref{lòkgyftdresdetfyguhijok}.  Assume that, for every~$u,v\in\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^N)$, the integrals 
\[
\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}} (u(x)-u(y))(v(x)-v(y))k_i(x,y)\,dx\,dy, \quad i\in\{1,2\}, 
\]
are absolutely convergent and satisfy
\[
\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}} (u(x)-u(y))(v(x)-v(y))k_1(x,y)\,dx\,dy = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}} (u(x)-u(y))(v(x)-v(y))k_2(x,y)\,dx\,dy. 
\]

Then,
\[
k_1=k_2\quad\mbox{ a.e. in }\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta.
\]

label: defrbgrnjkwdlqòshbasnjk
title: Proof
body_md:
We set $h:=k_1-k_2$.  Then, $h\in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta)$ and~$h(x, y)=h(y, x)$ for almost every~$(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta$. Moreover, the absolute convergence assumption implies that, for every~$u,v\in\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^N)$, 
\[
(u(x)-u(y))(v(x)-v(y))h(x,y) \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^{2N}).
\]
Hence, taking the difference of the two absolutely convergent integrals, we obtain that
\begin{equation}\label{defrbgrnjkwdlqòshbasnjk}
\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}}(u(x)-u(y))(v(x)-v(y))h(x,y)\,dx\,dy=0
\end{equation}
for every~$u,v\in\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^N)$.

Let $U,V\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be open sets such that $\overline U\cap\overline V=\varnothing$, and take $u\in C_c^{\infty}(U)$ and~$v\in C_c^{\infty}(V)$. Therefore, by~\eqref{defrbgrnjkwdlqòshbasnjk}, we get
\[
\begin{split}
0&=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}}(u(x)-u(y))(v(x)-v(y))h(x,y)\,dx\,dy\\
&=-\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}}u(x)v(y)h(x,y)\,dx\,dy-\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}}u(y)v(x)h(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\end{split}
\]
Notice that the two integrals on the right hand side are absolutely convergent. Indeed, their integrands are supported in $\mbox{supp}(u)\times \mbox{supp}(v)$ and~$\mbox{supp}(v)\times \mbox{supp}(u)$, respectively,  which are compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta$. Thus, their integrability follows from the fact that $h\in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta)$. 

By using the symmetry of $h$ and exchanging $x$ and~$y$ in the second integral, the two terms on the right hand side are equal.  Hence, for every~$u\in C_c^{\infty}(U)$ and~$v\in C_c^{\infty}(V)$,
\begin{equation}\label{èplqsdkowABJNCODKMsajcndbvzjknlkò}
\iint_{U\times V} u(x)v(y)h(x,y)\,dy\,dx=0.
\end{equation}

Since $h\in L^1_{loc}(U\times V)$, it defines a distribution $T_h\in\mathcal D'(U\times V)$ such that
\[
T_h(\varphi):=\iint_{U\times V} \varphi(x,y)\,h(x,y)\,dx\,dy,\quad{\mbox{for all }}\,\varphi\in C_c^{\infty}(U\times V).
\]
Accordingly, by~\eqref{èplqsdkowABJNCODKMsajcndbvzjknlkò}, we get
\[
T_h\left(u(x)v(y)\right)=0
\]
for every~$u\in C_c^{\infty}(U)$ and~$v\in C_c^{\infty}(V)$.

The uniqueness part of \cite[Theorem~5.1.1]{MR1996773}, applied to the zero distributions in $\mathcal D'(U)$ and~$\mathcal D'(V)$, implies that the only distribution~$T\in\mathcal D'(U\times V)$ satisfying
\[
T\left(u(x)v(y)\right)=0\quad\mbox{ for all } u\in C_c^{\infty}(U),\ v\in C_c^{\infty}(V),
\]
is the zero distribution. Hence
\[
T_h=0\quad\mbox{ in }\mathcal D'(U\times V).
\]
Since $T_h$ is the distribution induced by the locally integrable function $h$,  it follows that
\begin{equation}\label{vfcdxszaesrdtfghj}
h=0\quad\mbox{ a.e. in }U\times V.
\end{equation}

We now extend~\eqref{vfcdxszaesrdtfghj} to the whole $\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta$. To accomplish this goal, for every~$m\in\mathbb{N}$, we set
\[
K_m:=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2N} \mbox{ s.t. } |x|\leqslant m,\ |y|\leqslant m,\ |x-y|\geqslant \frac1m\right\}.
\]
Then $K_m$ is compact, $K_m\subset K_{m+1}$, and
\[
\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta=\bigcup_{m=1}^{+\infty} K_m.
\]
For every~$(x_0,y_0)\in K_m$, since $x_0\ne y_0$, there exist two open neighborhoods $U, V$ with $x_0\in U$, $y_0\in V$,  such that $\overline U\cap\overline V=\varnothing$. 

The sets $U\times V$ form an open cover of $K_m$. By compactness,  there exist finitely many such products $U_j\times V_j$ covering $K_m$. Since, thanks to~\eqref{vfcdxszaesrdtfghj}, $h=0$ a.e. in each $U_j\times V_j$, 
it follows that $h=0$ a.e. in $K_m$.
Since this holds for every~$m\in\mathbb{N}$, we conclude that $h=0$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta$, namely $k_1=k_2$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta$, as desired.

label: lemmatranslation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemmatranslation}
Let $k_A\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta)$ satisfy~\eqref{lòkgyftdresdetfyguhijok}. Assume that~\eqref{mnbhgvcfdxszxdfcgvhb} holds for every~$u, v\in\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^N)$.

Then, for every~$z\in\mathbb{R}^N$,
\[
k_A(x+z,y+z)=k_A(x,y)\quad\mbox{ for a.e.  }(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $z\in\mathbb{R}^N$, we set
\[
u_z(x):=u(x-z)\quad\mbox{ and }\quad v_z(x):=v(x-z).
\]
Since
\[
\mathcal F(u_z)(\xi)=e^{-iz\cdot\xi}\mathcal F(u)(\xi)\quad\mbox{ and }\quad \mathcal F(v_z)(\xi)=e^{-iz\cdot\xi}\mathcal F(v)(\xi),
\]
by Proposition~\ref{BAsymbol} we get
\[
\mathcal{B}_A(u_z,v_z)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}p_A(\xi)e^{-iz\cdot\xi}\widehat{u}(\xi) e^{iz\cdot\xi}\overline{\widehat{v}(\xi)}\,d\xi=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}p_A(\xi)\widehat{u}(\xi)\overline{\widehat{v}(\xi)}\,d\xi=\mathcal{B}_A(u,v).
\]
Accordingly,  applying~\eqref{mnbhgvcfdxszxdfcgvhb} to $u_z, v_z$ and changing variables, we obtain that

\[
\begin{split}
\mathcal{B}_A(u,v)&=\mathcal{B}_A(u_z,v_z)=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}}\left(u(x-z)-u(y-z)\right)\left(v(x-z)-v(y-z)\right) k_A(x,y)\,dx\,dy\\
&=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}}(u(x)-u(y))(v(x)-v(y))k_A(x+z,y+z)\,dx\,dy.
\end{split}
\]
On this account, we see that~$k_A(x+z,y+z)$ is another symmetric kernel which represents $\mathcal B_A$.  Thus,  Lemma~\ref{lemmauniq} yields the desired result.

label: lemmahomogn
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemmahomogn}
Let $k_A\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta)$ satisfy~\eqref{lòkgyftdresdetfyguhijok}. Assume that~\eqref{mnbhgvcfdxszxdfcgvhb} holds for every~$u, v\in\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^N)$.

Then, for every~$r>0$,

\]

label: jnkbhgvcfdxszfcgvhbjnkml,.
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $r>0$. We set
\[
u_r(x):=u(rx)\quad\mbox{ and }\quad v_r(x):=v(rx).
\]
Hence,
\[
\mathcal F(u_r)(\xi)=r^{-N}\mathcal F(u)\left(\frac{\xi}{r}\right) \quad\mbox{ and }\quad \mathcal F(v_r)(\xi)=r^{-N}\mathcal F(v)\left(\frac{\xi}{r}\right).
\]
By using Proposition~\ref{BAsymbol}, the change of variable~$\eta:=\xi/r$, and recalling that~$p_A(\xi)$ is homogeneous of degree~$2s$,  we infer that
\begin{equation}\label{jnkbhgvcfdxszfcgvhbjnkml,.}
\mathcal{B}_A(u_r,v_r)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}p_A(\xi)\widehat{u_r}(\xi)\overline{\widehat{v_r}(\xi)}\,d\xi=r^{-N}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}p_A(r\eta)\widehat{u}(\eta)\overline{\widehat{v}(\eta)}\,d\eta=r^{2s-N}\mathcal{B}_A(u,v).
\end{equation}

On the one hand, applying~\eqref{mnbhgvcfdxszxdfcgvhb} to $u_r, v_r$, and using the changes of variable~$X:=rx, Y:=ry$, we obtain that
\begin{equation}\label{mkljnhbgvfcdxszxdcfvg0}
\begin{split}
\mathcal{B}_A(u_r,v_r)&=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}}\left(u(rx)-u(ry)\right)\left(v(rx)-v(ry)\right)k_A(x,y)\,dx\,dy\\
&=r^{-2N}\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}}(u(X)-u(Y))(v(X)-v(Y))k_A\left(\frac{X}{r},\frac{Y}{r}\right)\,dX\,dY.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
On the other hand, by~\eqref{jnkbhgvcfdxszfcgvhbjnkml,.} and~\eqref{mnbhgvcfdxszxdfcgvhb} applied directly to $u$ and~$v$, 
\begin{equation}\label{mkljnhbgvfcdxszxdcfvg}
\mathcal{B}_A(u_r,v_r)=r^{2s-N}\mathcal{B}_A(u,v)=r^{2s-N}\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}}(u(X)-u(Y))(v(X)-v(Y))k_A(X,Y)\,dX\,dY.
\end{equation}
Thus, by~\eqref{mkljnhbgvfcdxszxdcfvg0},~\eqref{mkljnhbgvfcdxszxdcfvg}, and Lemma~\ref{lemmauniq}, we deduce that
\[
k_A\left(\frac{X}{r},\frac{Y}{r}\right) = r^{N+2s}k_A(X,Y)\quad\mbox{ for a.e. } (X,Y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta.
\]
Setting $x:=X/r$ and~$y:=Y/r$, we obtain the desired result.

label: PALKMND:01p
title: Proof
body_md:
We first show that there exists~$K_A\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\{0\})$ such that
\label{PALKMND:01p}
\begin{equation}\label{mnkjb hvcgfdxcghjnm}
\mbox{$k_A(x, y)=K_A(x-y)$}.
\end{equation}
To this end, we set~$\zeta:=x-y$ and~$q:=y$, and we define
\[
F(\zeta,q):=k_A(q+\zeta,q).
\]
Then, $F\in L^1_{loc}\left((\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}^N\right)$.  

We observe that, by Lemma~\ref{lemmatranslation},
for any~$z\in\mathbb{R}^N$,  
\[
k_A(q+\zeta+z,q+z)=k_A(q+\zeta,q)\quad\mbox{ for a.e.  }(\zeta,q)\in (\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}^N,
\]
namely,
\begin{equation}\label{lpkoijhugyftdreswrdtfgybhjnmkl,}
F(\zeta,q+z)=F(\zeta,q)\quad\mbox{ for a.e.  }(\zeta,q)\in (\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}^N.
\end{equation}
Thus, there exists a function $K_A\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\{0\})$ such that
\[
F(\zeta,q)=K_A(\zeta)\quad\mbox{ for a.e.  }(\zeta,q)\in (\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}^N.
\]
Returning to the original variables, we obtain~\eqref{mnkjb hvcgfdxcghjnm}.

By~\eqref{mnkjb hvcgfdxcghjnm} and Lemma~\ref{lemmahomogn}, we infer that, for every~$r>0$
and for a.e.~$(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2N}\setminus\Delta$,
\begin{equation}\label{bfdcxszsxedrctfvgybhunijm}
K_A(r(x-y))= k_A(rx,ry) = r^{-N-2s}k_A(x, y)= r^{-N-2s}K_A(x-y).
\end{equation}
Thus, by Lemma~\ref{lemmatecnico2.2} (here applied with $\gamma:=N+2s$) we infer that there exists $m_A\in L^1(\mathbb S^{N-1})$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{mn bjhvcgxfszddxfcvgbhnjkm,lò.à-}
K_A(\rho\theta)=\rho^{-N-2s}m_A(\theta)\quad\mbox{ for a.e.  }(\rho,\theta)\in(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb S^{N-1}.
\end{equation}
This is equivalent to
\[
K_A(z) =\frac{1}{|z|^{N+2s}} m_A\left(\frac{z}{|z|}\right)\quad\mbox{ for a.e.  }z\in\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\{0\}.
\]
Since $k_A(x,y)=k_A(y,x)$ for almost every~$(x,y)$, we have $K_A(z)=K_A(-z)$ for almost every~$z\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Therefore, by~\eqref{mn bjhvcgxfszddxfcvgbhnjkm,lò.à-} it follows that $m_A(\theta)=m_A(-\theta)$ for a.e.  $\theta\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$.
Moreover, recalling~\eqref{mnkjb hvcgfdxcghjnm}, we conclude that~\eqref{kernelconmATBD} holds. Finally, the uniqueness follows by Lemma~\ref{lemmauniq}.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{thmkernelstruct} and~\eqref{srdtfyguioplèòlkoijhugyftr1}, we infer that
\[
\lambda\leqslant m_A\left(\frac{x-y}{|x-y|}\right)|x-y|^{\alpha-2s}\leqslant\Lambda
\]
for almost every~$(x,y)$ such that $0<|x-y|\leqslant 1$. Namely,
\[
\lambda\leqslant m_A\left(\frac{z}{|z|}\right)|z|^{\alpha-2s}\leqslant\Lambda\quad\mbox{ for a.e.  $z$, with $0<|z|\leqslant 1$}.
\]
By writing $z:=\rho\theta$,
with $\rho\in(0,1]$ and~$\theta\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$,  we obtain that
\begin{equation}\label{+èpoi0u8y7t6r5e4w3aq<szdxfc}
\lambda\leqslant m_A(\theta)\rho^{\alpha-2s}\leqslant\Lambda\quad\mbox{ for a.e. } (\rho,\theta)\in(0,1]\times\mathbb S^{N-1}.
\end{equation}
The lower bound in~\eqref{+èpoi0u8y7t6r5e4w3aq<szdxfc} implies, in particular, that
\begin{equation}\label{nbhjgvcfdxsza<sxdcfvgb}
m_A(\theta)>0.
\end{equation}

Now, since~\eqref{+èpoi0u8y7t6r5e4w3aq<szdxfc} holds for almost every~$\rho\in(0,1)$, there exists an infinitesimal sequence~$\rho_j\subset(0,1)$ as~$j\to+\infty$
such that~\eqref{+èpoi0u8y7t6r5e4w3aq<szdxfc} holds at $\rho=\rho_j$ for every~$j\in\mathbb{N}$.

Assume first that $\alpha>2s$. Then,
\[
\lim_{j\to +\infty} m_A(\theta)\rho_j^{\alpha-2s} = 0,
\]
which contradicts the lower bound in~\eqref{+èpoi0u8y7t6r5e4w3aq<szdxfc}.

Suppose instead that $\alpha<2s$. By~\eqref{nbhjgvcfdxsza<sxdcfvgb}, we have
\[
\lim_{j\to +\infty} m_A(\theta)\rho_j^{\alpha-2s} = +\infty,
\]
which contradicts the upper bound in~\eqref{+èpoi0u8y7t6r5e4w3aq<szdxfc}.

From these considerations, we conclude that necessarily~$
\alpha=2s$.
Using this information in~\eqref{+èpoi0u8y7t6r5e4w3aq<szdxfc}, we get
\begin{equation}\label{lkjohiyguftdersawesrdtfyguhij}
\lambda\leqslant m_A(\theta)\leqslant\Lambda\quad\mbox{for a.e. }\theta\in\mathbb S^{N-1}.
\end{equation}

We now consider the case $|x-y|>1$. In this case, we use~\eqref{srdtfyguioplèòlkoijhugyftr2} and we see that
\begin{equation}\label{nhbgvfcdxsrdtfygbhujnkm}
m_A(\theta)\leqslant M\rho^{2s-\eta} \quad\mbox{ for a.e. } (\rho,\theta)\in(1,+\infty)\times\mathbb S^{N-1},
\end{equation}
If $\eta>2s$, then we can choose a diverging sequence~$\rho_j\in(1,+\infty)$ as~$j\to+\infty$ such that~\eqref{nhbgvfcdxsrdtfygbhujnkm} holds at~$\rho=\rho_j$ for all~$j\in\mathbb{N}$.
Accordingly, by~\eqref{lkjohiyguftdersawesrdtfyguhij} and~\eqref{nhbgvfcdxsrdtfygbhujnkm}, we have that
\[
\begin{split}
&\lambda\leqslant m_A(\theta)\leqslant M\rho_j^{2s-\eta} \ \mbox{ for all } j\in\mathbb{N}, \\
\mbox{ and } \quad &\lim_{j\to +\infty} M\rho_j^{2s-\eta} =0,
\end{split}
\]
which is a contradiction. Hence,  $\eta\leqslant 2s$.  Since $\eta>0$ by assumption, we infer that~$0<\eta\leqslant 2s$.

Therefore, choosing a sequence~$\rho_j \in(1,+\infty)$ such that
\[
\lim_{j\to +\infty} \rho_j = 1
\]
and~\eqref{nhbgvfcdxsrdtfygbhujnkm} holds at $\rho=\rho_j$ for all $j\in\mathbb{N}$, we get $m_A(\theta)\leqslant M$. 

Combining this with~\eqref{lkjohiyguftdersawesrdtfyguhij}, we conclude that
\[
\lambda\leqslant m_A(\theta)\leqslant\min\{\Lambda,M\} \quad\mbox{for a.e. }\theta\in\mathbb S^{N-1}.
\]
Gathering all these considerations, we obtain the desired claims.

label: pèkdowBH BJNKML
title: Proof
body_md:
We set $h\in\mathbb{R}^N$. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we get
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u(x)-u(x-h)|\,|v(x)-v(x-h)|\,dx\leqslant\|u(\cdot)-u(\cdot-h)\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}\|v(\cdot)-v(\cdot-h)\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}.
\]
If $|h|\leqslant 1$, then the fundamental theorem of calculus gives
\[
u(x)-u(x-h)=\int_0^1 h\cdot\nabla u(x-th)\,dt.
\]
Therefore,
\[
 \|u(\cdot)-u(\cdot-h)\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}\leqslant |h|\,\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)},
\]
and the same estimate holds for $v$.  Hence,  passing to polar coordinates, we have 
\begin{equation}\label{pèkdowBH BJNKML}
\begin{split}
&\int_{|h|\leqslant 1}\frac{|m(h/|h|)|}{|h|^{N+2s}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u(x)-u(x-h)|\,|v(x)-v(x-h)|\,dx\,dh\\
&\quad\leqslant\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}\int_{|h|\leqslant 1}\left|m\left(\frac{h}{|h|}\right)\right|\,|h|^{2-N-2s}\,dh\\
&\quad=\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)} \int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}|m(\omega)|\int_0^1 r^{2-N-2s}r^{N-1}\,dr\,d\omega\\
&\quad=\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}\|m\|_{L^1(\mathbb S^{N-1})}\int_0^1 r^{1-2s}\,dr
<+\infty.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
If instead $|h|>1$, then
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u(x)-u(x-h)|\,|v(x)-v(x-h)|\,dx\leqslant 4 \|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}\|v\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}.
\]
Thus, passing to polar coordinates, we have
\begin{equation}\label{esdr6tfygyhuijnkp}
\begin{split}
&\int_{|h|> 1}\frac{|m(h/|h|)|}{|h|^{N+2s}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u(x)-u(x-h)|\,|v(x)-v(x-h)|\,dx\,dh\\
&\quad\leqslant 4 \|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}\|v\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)} \int_{|h|> 1}\frac{|m(h/|h|)|}{|h|^{N+2s}}\, dh\\
&\quad\leqslant 4 \|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}\|v\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)} \|m\|_{L^1(\mathbb S^{N-1})}\int_1^{+\infty} r^{-1-2s}\,dr <+\infty.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Thus, combining~\eqref{Emdef},~\eqref{pèkdowBH BJNKML} and~\eqref{esdr6tfygyhuijnkp}, we obtain the desired result.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since
\[
1-\cos r=2\sin^2 \left(\frac r2\right),
\]
and~$|\sin t|\leqslant |t|$ for any $t\in\mathbb{R}$, we obtain that $0\leqslant 1-\cos r\leqslant \frac{r^2}{2}$. Hence, 
\[
0\leqslant\frac{1-\cos r}{r^{1+2s}}\leqslant\frac{r^{1-2s}}{2}.
\]
Since $s\in (0, 1)$, the right-hand side is integrable on $(0,1)$.

Moreover,  $0\leqslant 1-\cos r\leqslant2$ for $r>0$ and therefore
\[
0\leqslant\frac{1-\cos r}{r^{1+2s}}\leqslant\frac{2}{r^{1+2s}}.
\]
Since $s\in (0, 1)$, the right hand side is integrable on $(1, +\infty)$.
Therefore,  it follows that~$\kappa_s<+\infty$. Furthermore, since $1-\cos r\geqslant0$, and it is strictly positive for every~$r\notin2\pi\mathbb Z$, we infer that $\kappa_s>0$.

We now prove~\eqref{radscaling}.
If $t=0$, then~\eqref{radscaling} plainly follows.  If $t\ne0$, then the change of variable $\rho:=|t|r$ yields
\[
\int_0^{+\infty}\frac{1-\cos(rt)}{r^{1+2s}}\,dr=|t|^{2s}\int_0^{+\infty}\frac{1-\cos(\rho\,\mathrm{sgn}(t))}
{\rho^{1+2s}}\,d\rho =|t|^{2s}\int_0^{+\infty}\frac{1-\cos\rho}{\rho^{1+2s}}\,d\rho=\kappa_s|t|^{2s},
\]
as desired.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lemmafindiff}, we obtain that
\[
\begin{split}
\mathcal{E}_m(u,v) &= \frac{c_{N,s}}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{m(h/|h|)}{|h|^{N+2s}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}(u(x)-u(x-h))(v(x)-v(x-h)) \,dx \,dh\\
&= c_{N,s}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{m(h/|h|)}{|h|^{N+2s}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}(1-\cos(h\cdot\xi))\,\widehat{u}(\xi)\,\overline{\widehat{v}(\xi)}\, d\xi\, dh.
\end{split}
\]
We point out that the change of the order of integration is justified by Fubini's theorem. Indeed,
Lemma~\ref{lemmabsconv}, applied with $|m|$, gives the absolute convergence of the original double integral, and the above Fourier representation preserves this integrability. 

Hence, 
\[
\mathcal{E}_m(u,v) = c_{N,s}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\left(\;\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{m(h/|h|)}{|h|^{N+2s}}(1-\cos(h\cdot\xi))\,dh\right)\widehat{u}(\xi)\,\overline{\widehat{v}(\xi)}\,d\xi.
\]

We now use polar coordinate and write $h:=r\theta$, with $r>0$ and~$\theta\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$. Then,  by Lemma~\ref{lemmint}, we infer that
\[
c_{N,s}\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}m(\theta)\int_0^{+\infty} \frac{1-\cos(r\theta\cdot\xi)}{r^{1+2s}}\,dr\,d\theta = c_{N,s}\kappa_s\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}} m(\theta)|\theta\cdot\xi|^{2s}\,d\theta.
\]
Thus, recalling the definition of~$\psi_m$ in~\eqref{lòkjhgfdtresdtfyguhijokpl} we obtain the desired result.

We first show that $J_{N,s}$ is independent of the choice of $\omega\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$. To this end, let~$\omega_1,\omega_2\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$. Hence, there exists an orthogonal matrix
$R\in O(N)$ such that $R\omega_1=\omega_2$. Using the invariance of the
surface measure on $\mathbb S^{N-1}$ under rotations, we obtain that
\[
\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}|\omega_2\cdot\theta|^{2s}\,d\theta = \int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}|R\omega_1\cdot\theta|^{2s}\,d\theta = \int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}|\omega_1\cdot R^T\theta|^{2s}\,d\theta = \int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}|\omega_1\cdot\theta|^{2s}\,d\theta.
\]
This shows that $J_{N,s}$ does not depend on $\omega$.

Moreover,  the integrand is nonnegative and not identically zero on $\mathbb S^{N-1}$, since $|\omega\cdot\theta|^{2s}>0$ for every~$\theta$ in a neighborhood of $\omega$. Therefore, $J_{N,s}>0$.

It only remains to prove~\eqref{xsrdcftvgbhnjkm,lkmjnbhgv}. From~\eqref{lòkjhgfdtresdtfyguhijokpl}, used here with $m\equiv 1$, we have that, for any~$\xi\in\mathbb{R}^N$ with $\xi\ne 0$,
\[
\psi_1(\xi) = c_{N,s}\kappa_s|\xi|^{2s}\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\left|\frac{\xi}{|\xi|}\cdot\theta\right|^{2s}\,d\theta.
\]
By the independence of $J_{N,s}$ from the direction, we can write
\[
\psi_1(\xi) = c_{N,s}\kappa_sJ_{N,s}|\xi|^{2s}.
\]

Accordingly, the normalization in~\eqref{E1normalization} and Proposition~\ref{BAsymbol}, used here with $A:=I$, show that
\begin{eqnarray*}&&
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |\xi|^{2s}\,\widehat{u}(\xi)\overline{\widehat{v}(\xi)}\,d\xi = \mathcal{B}_{I}(u,v) =  \mathcal{E}_1(u,v) \\&&\qquad= \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\psi_1(\xi)\widehat{u}(\xi)\overline{\widehat{v}(\xi)}\, d\xi
=
c_{N,s}\kappa_sJ_{N,s}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |\xi|^{2s}\,\widehat{u}(\xi)\overline{\widehat{v}(\xi)}\,d\xi ,
\end{eqnarray*}
which entails that~$c_{N,s}\kappa_sJ_{N,s}=1$, as desired.

title: Proof
body_md:
We first consider the case $N=1$. In this case, $A=A_{11}$ and $\mathbb S^0=\{-1,1\}$. Hence, for every~$\omega,\theta\in\mathbb S^0$, we have $|\omega\theta|=1$ and $\theta\cdot A\theta=A_{11}$. Therefore,
\[
\frac{\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb S^0}(\theta\cdot A\theta)
|\omega\theta|^{2s}\,d\theta}
{\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb S^0}|\omega\theta|^{2s}\,d\theta}
=A_{11}.
\]
Moreover, since $|\omega|^2=1$, we have
\[
\frac{\operatorname{tr}(A)+2s\,\omega\cdot A\omega}{1+2s} = \frac{A_{11}+2sA_{11}}{1+2s} =A_{11}. 
\] The last two displays establish
\eqref{lsqkdJNCHUBSAKMOXxcsdjbhvhn} when $N=1$.

From now on we suppose that $N\geqslant 2$. Let $\omega\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$ and define
\begin{equation}\label{dretfyghuijoklpèòlppkoijuhgy}
F_\omega(A):=\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}(\theta\cdot A\theta)|\omega\cdot\theta|^{2s}\,d\theta =\sum_{i,j=1}^N A_{ij}\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\theta_i\theta_j|\omega\cdot\theta|^{2s}\,d\theta.
\end{equation}
We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{pèkljniopjhgvftyrdszdwez}
F_\omega(A) = \frac{J_{N,s}}{N+2s}\left(\operatorname{tr}(A)+2s\,\omega\cdot A\omega\right).
\end{equation}
We first prove~\eqref{pèkljniopjhgvftyrdszdwez} in the case $\omega=e_1$.  By~\eqref{dretfyghuijoklpèòlppkoijuhgy},  we infer that
\begin{equation}\label{opkjoikjnio0ijohutfde4eswe4e5dstyh}
F_{e_1}(A)=\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}(\theta\cdot A\theta)|\theta_1|^{2s}\,d\theta =\sum_{i,j=1}^N A_{ij}\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\theta_i\theta_j|\theta_1|^{2s}\,d\theta.
\end{equation}

Let $i\ne j$. We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{,lkjnhbgvfctdxrctfvgbhnm}
\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\theta_i\theta_j|\theta_1|^{2s}\,d\theta=0.
\end{equation}
Indeed, since $i\neq j$, at least one of the two indices $i$ and~$j$ is different from $1$. Let $k\in\{i,j\}$ be such an index, and consider the reflection
\[
R_k(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k,\dots,\theta_N) = (\theta_1,\dots,-\theta_k,\dots,\theta_N).
\]
The map $R_k$ preserves both the sphere and the surface measure. Moreover, since $k\ne 1$, we have $|(R_k\theta)_1 |^{2s}=|\theta_1|^{2s}$.
On the other hand, since exactly one of the two factors $\theta_i,\theta_j$ changes its sign, it follows that
\[
(R_k\theta)_i(R_k\theta)_j=-\theta_i\theta_j.
\]
Therefore, by using the change of variable $\theta\mapsto R_k\theta$, we get
\[
\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\theta_i\theta_j|\theta_1|^{2s}\,d\theta = \int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}(R_k\theta)_i(R_k\theta)_j
|(R_k\theta)_1|^{2s}\,d\theta = -\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\theta_i\theta_j|\theta_1|^{2s}\,d\theta.
\]
This proves the claim in~\eqref{,lkjnhbgvfctdxrctfvgbhnm}.

For the case $i=j$, we set
\[
a:=\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\theta_1^2|\theta_1|^{2s} d\theta.
\]
Moreover, we notice that the coordinates $\theta_2,\dots,\theta_N$ play a symmetric role. Indeed,  any permutation of these coordinates preserves the sphere, the surface measure, and the weight $|\theta_1|^{2s}$. Hence,
\[
\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\theta_2^2|\theta_1|^{2s}\,d\theta = \cdots = \int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\theta_N^2|\theta_1|^{2s}\,d\theta=:b .
\]
Combining this with~\eqref{opkjoikjnio0ijohutfde4eswe4e5dstyh} and~\eqref{,lkjnhbgvfctdxrctfvgbhnm}, we obtain that
\begin{equation}\label{nbhgvfcdxcfvgybhnjm}
F_{e_1}(A) = \sum_{i=1}^N A_{ii}\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\theta_i^2|\theta_1|^{2s}\,d\theta = a A_{11}+b\sum_{i=2}^N A_{ii}.
\end{equation}

Now, since
\[
A_{11}=e_1\cdot A e_1\quad\mbox{ and }\quad\sum_{i=2}^N A_{ii}=\operatorname{tr}(A)-e_1\cdot A e_1,
\]
we can write~\eqref{nbhgvfcdxcfvgybhnjm} as
\[
F_{e_1}(A) = b\,\operatorname{tr}(A)+(a-b)\,e_1\cdot A e_1.
\]
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}\label{dfvgbhnjkml,vhbnjkm,}
F_{e_1}(A) = \alpha\operatorname{tr}(A)+\beta\,e_1\cdot A e_1,
\end{equation}
where $\alpha:=b$ and~$\beta:=a-b$ depend only on $N$ and~$s$. 

We now determine $\alpha$ and~$\beta$. Recalling~\eqref{JNsdefn}, since $\theta\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$, we get
\begin{equation}\label{è+òplkoijhugyftrdeswasrdtfyguhj}
J_{N,s} = F_{e_1}(I) = N\alpha+\beta.
\end{equation}
On the other hand,  choosing~$A$ to be the matrix with entries $A_{ij}=\delta_{i, 1}\delta_{j, 1}$,  where $\delta_{ij}$ denotes the Kronecker delta. Thus, we have $\theta\cdot A\theta = |\theta_1|^2$, and hence
\begin{equation}\label{qaw3edr5tghyujkolò}
F_{e_1}(A) = \int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}|\theta_1|^{2s+2}\,d\theta = \alpha+\beta.
\end{equation}
It only remains to compute the latter integral. By using spherical coordinates with respect to the
axis $e_1$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{xsdcfvgbhnjkml,.}
\begin{split}
&J_{N,s} = |\mathbb S^{N-2}|\int_{-1}^{1}|t|^{2s}(1-t^2)^{\frac{N-3}{2}}\,dt,\\
\mbox{ and }\quad&\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}|\theta_1|^{2s+2}\,d\theta = |\mathbb S^{N-2}|\int_{-1}^{1}|t|^{2s+2}(1-t^2)^{\frac{N-3}{2}}\,dt.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
By symmetry, it is enough to consider the integrals on $(0,1)$.  We set
\[
f(t):=t^{2s+1}(1-t^2)^{\frac{N-1}{2}}.
\]
We notice that $f(0)=f(1)=0$, and~$f'\in L^1(0,1)$. Thus, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus yields
\[
0=f(1)-f(0)=\int_0^1 f'(t)\,dt = (2s+1)\int_0^1 t^{2s}(1-t^2)^{\frac{N-1}{2}}\,dt -(N-1)\int_0^1 t^{2s+2}(1-t^2)^{\frac{N-3}{2}}\,dt.
\]
By using the identity
\[
(1-t^2)^{\frac{N-1}{2}}=(1-t^2)^{\frac{N-3}{2}}-t^2(1-t^2)^{\frac{N-3}{2}},
\]
we conclude that
\[
(2s+1)\int_0^1 t^{2s}(1-t^2)^{\frac{N-3}{2}}\,dt = (2s+N)\int_0^1 t^{2s+2}(1-t^2)^{\frac{N-3}{2}}\,dt.
\]
Accordingly, by~\eqref{xsdcfvgbhnjkml,.}, we get
\[
\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}|\theta_1|^{2s+2}\,d\theta = \frac{2s+1}{N+2s}J_{N,s}.
\]
Combining this with~\eqref{qaw3edr5tghyujkolò},  we have that
\begin{equation}\label{lpojkhiu8ytfdrewaewsdrftgyhj}
\alpha+\beta=\frac{2s+1}{N+2s}J_{N,s}.
\end{equation}
Now, subctracting~\eqref{lpojkhiu8ytfdrewaewsdrftgyhj} from~\eqref{è+òplkoijhugyftrdeswasrdtfyguhj}, we get
\[
(N-1)\alpha = \frac{N-1}{N+2s}J_{N,s},
\]
namely
\[
\alpha=\frac{J_{N,s}}{N+2s}\quad\mbox{ and }\quad \beta = J_{N,s}-N\alpha = \frac{2s J_{N,s}}{N+2s}.
\]
Substituting these values in~\eqref{dfvgbhnjkml,vhbnjkm,}, we get
\begin{equation}\label{xsdcfvgrbtdhnyjhtbgrsvfdcsxa}
F_{e_1}(A) = \frac{J_{N,s}}{N+2s}\left(\operatorname{tr}(A)+2s\,e_1\cdot A e_1\right).
\end{equation}
This proves the desired claim~\eqref{pèkljniopjhgvftyrdszdwez} when $\omega=e_1$.

We now take $\omega\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$ and~$R_\omega\in O(N)$ such that 
\begin{equation}\label{àòèplkoijugytdreswasrdtfgyhj}
R_\omega e_1 =\omega.
\end{equation}
We set
\begin{equation}\label{vncmwqur385784SDFGH87r34y89to}
A_\omega:=R_\omega^{-1} A R_\omega = R_\omega^{T} A R_\omega.
\end{equation}
Thus, $A_\omega^T = A_\omega$. Hence, using the change of variable~$\theta := R_\omega\eta$, and recalling~\eqref{dretfyghuijoklpèòlppkoijuhgy},
\eqref{opkjoikjnio0ijohutfde4eswe4e5dstyh} and~\eqref{àòèplkoijugytdreswasrdtfgyhj},
\[
\begin{split}&
F_\omega(A)= \int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}(R_\omega\eta\cdot A R_\omega\eta)|R_\omega e_1\cdot R_\omega\eta|^{2s}\,d\eta = \int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\eta\cdot (R_\omega^T A R_\omega)\eta \,|e_1 \cdot\eta|^{2s}\,d\eta\\
&\qquad\qquad= \int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\eta\cdot A_\omega \eta \,|\eta_1|^{2s}\,d\eta =  F_{e_1}(A_\omega).
\end{split}
\]
From this and~\eqref{xsdcfvgrbtdhnyjhtbgrsvfdcsxa}, we infer tht
\begin{equation}\label{cnewuti4uitkjt47838roihjsdfgfjie54oyu}
F_\omega(A)= \frac{J_{N,s}}{N+2s}\left(\operatorname{tr}(A_\omega)+2s\,e_1\cdot A_\omega e_1\right).
\end{equation}

Now we notice that, by~\eqref{àòèplkoijugytdreswasrdtfgyhj}
and~\eqref{vncmwqur385784SDFGH87r34y89to},
\[
e_1\cdot A_\omega e_1 =   e_1\cdot R_\omega^{T} A\,R_\omega e_1 = R_\omega e_1\cdot A\,R_\omega e_1 = \omega\cdot A \omega 
\]
and
\[
\begin{split}&
\operatorname{tr}(A_\omega)= \sum_{i=1}^N (R_\omega^T A R_\omega)_{ii} = \sum_{i,j,k=1}^N (R_\omega)_{ji} A_{jk} (R_\omega)_{ki}\\
&\qquad= \sum_{j,k=1}^N A_{jk} \sum_{i=1}^N (R_\omega)_{ji}(R_\omega)_{ki} = \sum_{j,k=1}^N A_{jk}\,\delta_{jk}= \sum_{j=1}^N A_{jj}= \operatorname{tr}(A).
\end{split}
\]
Combining these pieces of information with~\eqref{cnewuti4uitkjt47838roihjsdfgfjie54oyu}, we get
\[
F_\omega(A)= \frac{J_{N,s}}{N+2s}\left(\operatorname{tr}(A)+2s\,\omega\cdot A\omega\right),
\] which is
the claim in~\eqref{pèkljniopjhgvftyrdszdwez}.

Dividing by $J_{N,s}$ and recalling the definition in~\eqref{dretfyghuijoklpèòlppkoijuhgy}, we obtain the desired identity~\eqref{lsqkdJNCHUBSAKMOXxcsdjbhvhn}.

and
\[

\]

We now recall the following standard equalities for~$f$, $g\in \mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^N)$:
\[
\widehat{fg}(\zeta)=(2\pi)^{-N/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\widehat f(\eta)\widehat g(\zeta-\eta)\,d\eta\quad\mbox{ and }\quad \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}f(x)g(x)\,dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\widehat f(\zeta)\widehat g(-\zeta)\,d\zeta.
\]
Therefore, by using~\eqref{defnfrgradient}, and since
\[
\widehat{D_j^sv}(-\zeta) = i q_j(-\zeta)\widehat v(-\zeta)= -i q_j(\zeta)\widehat v(-\zeta),
\]
we obtain that
\[
\begin{split}
I_C[u,v]&= \sum_{j,k=1}^N \ \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\widehat{C_{jk}D_k^su}(\zeta)\widehat{D_j^sv}(-\zeta)\,d\zeta\\& =(2\pi)^{-N/2}\sum_{j,k=1}^N \ \iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2N}}\widehat C_{jk}(\eta)\widehat{D_k^su}(\zeta-\eta)\,

We now fix $\eta,\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^N$ and we set $a:=\zeta-\eta$. Then,
\begin{equation}\label{awesrdtfyguiopè+òlpkojihughf}

We claim that, for $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^N$,
\begin{equation}\label{pokjhgfdre4356789i0opl}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{1-\cos(h\cdot\xi)}{|h|^{N+2s}}\, dh = \frac{|\xi|^{2s}}{c_{N,s}},
\end{equation}
Indeed, by \cite[3.381, n.4,  page 348]{MR3307944} we get
\[
|h|^{-N-2s} = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\frac N2+s)} \int_0^{+\infty} t^{\frac N2+s-1}e^{-t|h|^2}\, dt.
\]
Moreover, \cite[3.433, page 363]{MR3307944}, here applied with $n=1$ and $p=-s$, gives
\[
\int_0^{+\infty}\frac{1-e^{-r}}{r^{1+s}} \,dr =\frac{\Gamma(1-s)}{s},
\]
By using the latter identity and the change of variable $r:=|\xi|^2/(4t)$, we obtain that, for $\xi\ne0$,
\[
\begin{split}&
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{1-\cos(h\cdot\xi)}{|h|^{N+2s}} \,dh = \frac{\pi^{N/2}}{\Gamma(\frac N2+s)} \int_0^{+\infty} t^{s-1}
\left(1-e^{-\frac{|\xi|^2}{4t}}\right) \,dt = \frac{\pi^{N/2}|\xi|^{2s}}{2^{2s}\Gamma(\frac N2+s)}\int_0^{+\infty}\frac{1-e^{-r}}{r^{1+s}} \,dr\\
&\qquad\qquad=\frac{\pi^{N/2}\Gamma(1-s)}{2^{2s}s\,\Gamma(\frac N2+s)}|\xi|^{2s}=\frac{|\xi|^{2s}}{c_{N,s}},
\end{split}
\]
which proves \eqref{pokjhgfdre4356789i0opl}.

Now, by Plancherel's identity, the translation property of the Fourier transform and~\eqref{pokjhgfdre4356789i0opl}, we have
\[
\begin{split}

&=\frac{c_{N,s}}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{1}{|h|^{N+2s}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|1-e^{-ih\cdot\xi}|^2\widehat u(\xi)\overline{\widehat v(\xi)} \,d\xi\, dh\\
&=c_{N,s}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\widehat u(\xi)\overline{\widehat v(\xi)}\left(\,\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{1-\cos(h\cdot\xi)}{|h|^{N+2s}} \,dh
\right)\,d\xi \\&= \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\xi|^{2s}\widehat u(\xi)\overline{\widehat v(\xi)}\, d\xi.

\]
We point out that the use of Fubini's theorem is justified by \eqref{pokjhgfdre4356789i0opl} and the rapid decay
of both~$\widehat u$ and~$\widehat v$. Moreover, by \eqref{defnfrgradient} and the Plancherel's identity, we have that
\begin{eqnarray*}&&

Suppose by contradiction that there exists $R_0>0$ such that

\begin{equation}\label{òlpèokiugtfrdesw}

\end{equation}
Since the fractional gradient is homogeneous of degree $s$, we have that
\[

\]

\[

\]

\begin{equation}\label{lèpokijuhygftde43waser6fyguyhjo}

\end{equation}

We now estimate the right-hand side of
\eqref{mnbhgvcfdxszxdfcgvhb}. For any~$z\in\mathbb{R}^N$, we define
\[
G(z):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\phi(x+z)-\phi(x)|^2 dx.
\]
By the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have
\[
\phi(x+z)-\phi(x) = \int_0^1 z\cdot\nabla\phi(x+tz) dt.
\]
Hence, by using Minkowski inequality, we get that
\[
\|\phi(\cdot+z)-\phi\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}\leqslant |z|\|\nabla\phi\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}.
\]
Therefore, we obtain that
\[

where the last integral is finite since we assumed $\alpha\in(0,2)$. Thus, there exists a constant~$C_{R_0}>0$,
independent of $R$, such that

where $C>0$ is independent of $R$. 

Moreover, by \eqref{cxzsedrftyhujiko098765r4e3wq2a<}, we get

body_md:
Let $d\sigma$ denote the surface measure on $\mathbb S^{N-1}$, and take $0<\alpha<\beta<+\infty$.  When $N=1$, we use the notation $\mathbb S^0=\{-1,1\}$, endowed with the $0$ dimensional Hausdorff measure, so that the usual polar integration formula remains true.

We define
\begin{equation}\label{òàèù+plkoijhugyftdresdtfygh}
G(\rho,\theta):=\rho^\gamma K(\rho\theta),\quad\mbox{ for }(\rho,\theta)\in(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb S^{N-1}.
\end{equation}
We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{q23456789olkmnbvcdse4567uikmnb }
G\in L^1\left((\alpha,\beta)\times\mathbb S^{N-1}\right).
\end{equation}
Indeed, set
\[
C_{\alpha,\beta}:=\max_{\rho\in[\alpha,\beta]}\rho^{\gamma-N+1}<+\infty.
\]
Since $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N:\alpha\leqslant |x|\leqslant\beta\}\subset\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\{0\}$ is compact, and~$K\in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\{0\})$,  by using the change of variable $x:=\rho\theta$, we infer that
\[
\begin{split}&
\int_\alpha^\beta\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}|G(\rho,\theta)| d\sigma(\theta) d\rho= \int_\alpha^\beta\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\rho^\gamma |K(\rho\theta)| d\sigma(\theta) d\rho\leqslant C_{\alpha,\beta}\int_\alpha^\beta\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}|K(\rho\theta)|\rho^{N-1}\,d\sigma(\theta)\,d\rho\\
&\qquad\qquad=\int_{\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N:\alpha\leqslant |x|\leqslant\beta\}} |K(x)|\,dx <+\infty,
\end{split}
\]
thus establishing~\eqref{q23456789olkmnbvcdse4567uikmnb }.

We now use the homogeneity assumption. Fix $r>0$. By~\eqref{ò.,adklms<cgvysjnzklm,} we get
\[
K(r\rho\theta)=r^{-\gamma}K(\rho\theta)\quad\mbox{ for a.e. } (\rho,\theta)\in(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb S^{N-1}.
\]
Accordingly, we have
\begin{equation}\label{òlkjihugyftdxrcfv}
G(r\rho,\theta)=(r\rho)^\gamma K(r\rho\theta)=r^\gamma\rho^\gamma r^{-\gamma}K(\rho\theta)=G(\rho,\theta)\quad\mbox{ for a.e. } (\rho,\theta)\in(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb S^{N-1}.
\end{equation}

We claim that, in fact,
\begin{equation}\label{.òlpkojihugyfctdxrszexdcfvgbhn}
G(r\rho,\theta)=G(\rho,\theta) \quad\mbox{ for a.e. } (r, \rho,\theta)\in(0,+\infty)\times (0, +\infty)\times\mathbb S^{N-1}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, define
\[
E:=\left\{(r,\rho,\theta)\in(0,+\infty)\times (0, +\infty)\times\mathbb S^{N-1} \mbox{ s.t. } G(r\rho,\theta)\ne G(\rho,\theta)\right\}.
\]
For every fixed $r>0$, let
\[
E_r:=\left\{(\rho,\theta)\in(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb S^{N-1} \mbox{ s.t. } (r,\rho,\theta)\in E\right\}.
\]
By~\eqref{òlkjihugyftdxrcfv}, it follows that $E_r$ has zero
measure in~$(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb S^{N-1} $ for every~$r>0$. Therefore,
by Tonelli's theorem applied to $\chi_E$, it follows that
\[
\int_0^{+\infty}\int_0^{+\infty}\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}} \chi_E(r,\rho,\theta) d\sigma(\theta)\,d\rho\,dr =\int_0^{+\infty}\left[\int_0^{+\infty}\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\chi_E(r,\rho,\theta) d\sigma(\theta)\,d\rho\right]dr=0.
\]
Thus, $E$ has measure zero. This proves the claim in~\eqref{.òlpkojihugyfctdxrszexdcfvgbhn}.

We now set~$s:=r\rho$ and we have from~\eqref{.òlpkojihugyfctdxrszexdcfvgbhn} that
\[
G(s,\theta)=G(\rho,\theta)\quad\mbox{ for a.e. } (s, \rho,\theta)\in(0,+\infty)\times (0, +\infty)\times\mathbb S^{N-1}.
\]
Applying Fubini's theorem once more, we deduce that for almost every~$(\rho,\theta)\in(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb S^{N-1}$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{kmjnbhgvcfdxszxfcghvbjnkml,ò.}
G(s,\theta)=G(\rho,\theta)\quad\mbox{for a.e. }s\in(\alpha,\beta).
\end{equation}

We now define
\[
m(\theta):=\frac1{\beta-\alpha}\int_\alpha^\beta G(s,\theta)\,ds
.\]
Thanks to~\eqref{q23456789olkmnbvcdse4567uikmnb }, we see that~$m\in L^1(\mathbb S^{N-1})$.

Finally,  by~\eqref{kmjnbhgvcfdxszxfcghvbjnkml,ò.}, we deduce that, for almost every~$(\rho,\theta)\in (0, +\infty)\times\mathbb S^{N-1}$, 
\[
m(\theta)= \frac1{\beta-\alpha}\int_\alpha^\beta G(\rho,\theta)\,ds=G(\rho,\theta).
\]
Recalling~\eqref{òàèù+plkoijhugyftdresdtfygh}, we obtain the desired result.
